items.title: L3: Personal statement, CV or form
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Civil Service adverts ask for different kinds of written application, and the advert tells you which one to use. A personal statement is a piece of writing, often with a word limit, in which you explain how you meet the criteria. A CV is a short summary of your work, study and other experience, usually listing the most recent first. Some adverts ask for both. Others use an application form with a few separate questions, each with its own limit on length. Some campaigns ask for a short written answer on one or two behaviours instead of a personal statement. Whatever the format, assessors are looking for evidence. Evidence means a specific example showing what you did, not a general claim. A personal statement works best when it is organised around the criteria in the advert, so that the assessor can find each one easily. Keep to the word limit, because text beyond it may not be read. Use plain English and short paragraphs. Check spelling and grammar, and read the statement aloud or ask someone to read it, since a careless mistake can suggest a lack of attention to detail, which matters in administrative jobs. Save a copy of what you submit, so that you can use it again to prepare for an interview.

questions.prompt: What is a personal statement in a Civil Service application?

options.text: A piece of writing where you explain how you meet the criteria in the advert
A reference letter written by your last employer about your character
A list of your qualifications and the dates that you gained them
A form that confirms your name, address and national insurance number

questions.hint: It is your own account of how you meet the criteria.

questions.prompt: How does a CV usually list your experience?

options.text: In alphabetical order of the employer name
With the most recent job or activity first
By the salary paid in each job from lowest to highest
With the oldest job or activity first

questions.hint: Most CVs put the most recent first.

questions.prompt: Why does the advert say which type of application to submit?

options.text: Different campaigns assess different things in different formats
All campaigns share the same format and the advert only repeats it
The format is chosen by each applicant when they apply
The department changes the format after the closing date

questions.hint: Formats differ between campaigns.

questions.prompt: What do assessors mean by evidence?

options.text: A certificate from a course that you took some years ago
A general statement that you are hard-working and reliable
A specific example that shows what you actually did
A reference from a friend saying that you are suitable

questions.hint: Evidence is specific, not general.

questions.prompt: Why is it helpful to organise a personal statement around the criteria?

options.text: A statement without headings is automatically sifted out
The statement will be scored by a computer that looks for headings
The criteria are always scored equally, whatever you write
The assessor can find your evidence for each criterion easily

questions.hint: Structure helps the assessor match your evidence.

questions.prompt: What can happen to text that goes beyond the word limit?

options.text: It is deleted and a note is made on your profile
It is read and earns bonus marks
It is sent to a second assessor
It may not be read

questions.hint: Over-length text may be ignored.

questions.prompt: Why might spelling mistakes matter more in an administrative role?

options.text: They mean you are not eligible to work in the UK
They reduce the salary that can be offered
They show that you have not studied at university
They can suggest a lack of attention to detail

questions.hint: Admin work depends on accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which habit helps you catch errors in a statement?

options.text: Leaving it unchecked so that the first draft sounds natural
Reading it aloud or asking someone to read it
Copying it from a template found online
Reading it only once, quickly, just before submitting

questions.hint: A fresh pair of eyes catches mistakes.

questions.prompt: Why save a copy of what you submit?

options.text: You must send the copy to the panel on request
A copy is needed to claim your travel costs
The website deletes your answers after the closing date
You can use it to prepare for an interview

questions.hint: Your answers show which examples you chose.

questions.prompt: What may a short written answer on a behaviour replace?

options.text: The pre-employment checks
The interview panel
The closing date
A personal statement

questions.hint: Some campaigns use behaviour answers instead of a statement.

items.title: L3: What each stage is designed to find out
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Each stage of Civil Service recruitment has a purpose, and knowing it helps you prepare. The application and sift check that you meet the essential criteria and show evidence of the behaviours or experience the job needs. It is a way of reducing a large number of applicants to a smaller number for the next stage. Online tests, where they are used, measure ability, such as how well you understand written information or work with numbers. They are standard for every candidate, so they give a fair way to compare people who have different backgrounds. The interview looks at behaviours and strengths in more depth, and it allows the panel to ask follow-up questions that a form cannot. It also lets you show how you communicate. The pre-employment checks do not test your ability. They confirm that what you have said is true and that you are allowed to work in the job, including any security requirement. The start date marks the end of the process and the beginning of induction. Because of this, a weakness at one stage cannot always be balanced by a strength at another. A strong interview does not rescue an application that failed the sift, because the sift comes first and decides who goes on. Prepare for each stage separately, using the advert to learn what is assessed.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the sift?

options.text: To confirm the identity and nationality of every applicant before interview
To decide which department each successful applicant will join
To give every applicant a score that is used to set their salary
To reduce a large number of applicants to a smaller number who meet the criteria

questions.hint: The sift narrows the field to those who meet the bar.

questions.prompt: What do online tests usually measure?

options.text: Qualifications, such as the grades you got at school
Personality, such as whether you prefer working alone or in a team
Ability, such as understanding information or working with numbers
Loyalty, such as how long you stayed in your last job

questions.hint: Tests measure ability.

questions.prompt: Why are tests a fair way of comparing people from different backgrounds?

options.text: Every candidate takes the same standard test
Tests favour those who studied at university
Tests allow candidates to choose the questions they prefer
The tests are different for each candidate so none can compare

questions.hint: Standardisation makes the comparison fair.

questions.prompt: What can an interview do that a form usually cannot?

options.text: Prove that your references are correct
Show the panel your exam certificates and training record in detail
Allow the panel to ask follow-up questions
Test your typing speed in real time

questions.hint: Interviews allow follow-up.

questions.prompt: What do pre-employment checks confirm?

options.text: That what you have said is true and that you may work in the job
That you will be happy in the team you join
That your interview answers were scored correctly
That you are better suited to the job than the other applicants who applied

questions.hint: The checks verify facts rather than test ability.

questions.prompt: What does the start date mark?

options.text: The deadline for the pre-employment checks
The date of the last test in the process
The end of the process and the beginning of induction
The beginning of the sift and the end of the advert period

questions.hint: It is when the new job begins.

questions.prompt: Why can a strong interview not rescue an application that failed the sift?

options.text: The sift decides who goes on to the interview
Panel members cannot read the sift scores
The sift is repeated after the interview
The interview is never held for sifted-out applicants but the panel will always score highly

questions.hint: Only candidates who pass the sift reach the interview.

questions.prompt: Why should you prepare for each stage separately?

options.text: Each stage is held by a different department
Each stage assesses something different
Each stage is marked by the same person
Each stage uses the same questions in a new order

questions.hint: Stages test different things.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to find out what each stage will assess?

options.text: Look at last year's successful applications
Ask people who have worked in the department
Read the advert and any invitation emails
Wait until the day and see what happens

questions.hint: The advert and emails say what is assessed.

questions.prompt: What does a standard test give an employer that an interview alone may not?

options.text: A way to avoid asking any other questions
A replacement for pre-employment checks
A consistent measure of ability for every candidate
A guarantee of exactly who will perform best once they are in the job

questions.hint: Tests are consistent across candidates.

items.title: L3: Reasons for being sifted out and what to do
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Many people are sifted out of their first few Civil Service applications. It does not mean that you are unsuitable. There are common reasons, and most can be fixed. One reason is that you did not meet an essential criterion, or did not make it clear that you did. Another is that your examples were vague. A statement such as I am a good team player gives the assessor nothing to score. A third reason is that the answer did not match the question. For instance, a question about a time you handled a difficult customer needs an example of that, not a general description of your people skills. A fourth reason is a competitive campaign, where the pass mark was raised because many people scored well. A fifth is rushing, which leads to errors or unfinished answers. To improve, ask for feedback. Many departments provide it, and it tells you where you lost marks. Look again at the advert and your answers and compare them. Write down several examples from your life, such as work, volunteering or caring, and practise setting them out using STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Ask a friend to read your answers. Then apply again. Many people succeed on their third, fourth or fifth application after learning from earlier ones.

questions.prompt: What does being sifted out say about you?

options.text: That your references were unsatisfactory
That you are unsuitable for any Civil Service job and should not reapply
That the department has banned you from reapplying
That your application did not meet the bar for this campaign

questions.hint: It relates to one application, not you as a person.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common reason for being sifted out?

options.text: Giving vague examples that cannot be scored
Submitting the application well before the deadline
Applying early in the advert period
Using plain English in your answers

questions.hint: Vague examples earn few marks.

questions.prompt: Which statement gives the assessor least to score?

options.text: I am a good team player
I organised the rota for six volunteers and swapped shifts when two were ill
I wrote the minutes of each meeting and sent them out within a day
I checked 40 forms each week and corrected errors before they were sent on

questions.hint: General claims cannot be scored.

questions.prompt: Why does an answer fail if it does not match the question?

options.text: Assessors are not allowed to read beyond the first sentence
The system rejects any answer containing the wrong keyword
The assessor can only score what answers the question asked
The assessor must stop scoring after the first mistake

questions.hint: Marks are given for answering the question.

questions.prompt: How can a competitive campaign lead to a good answer being sifted out?

options.text: Answers longer than average are removed
The best answers are held back for later rounds
The assessors are told to reject a fixed number of applications
The pass mark may be raised because many people score well

questions.hint: A high number of strong applicants can raise the mark.

questions.prompt: What is the first useful step after an unsuccessful sift?

options.text: Ask for feedback
Wait several years before applying again
Complain to the Prime Minister

questions.hint: Feedback shows where marks were lost.

questions.prompt: Why compare your answers with the advert after feedback?

options.text: You can see where your evidence did not match the criteria
You can check whether the advert was altered
You can find out the names of the other applicants
You can copy sentences from the advert into your next answer

questions.hint: Matching answers to criteria is the key skill.

questions.prompt: What does STAR help you to do?

options.text: Work out the pass mark that applies to your application
Calculate a salary
Structure an example clearly
Check a security level

questions.hint: STAR is a structure for examples.

questions.prompt: What can writing several examples in advance help with?

options.text: Memorising a script for all situations
Being sure that every answer is identical
Using them again for different questions and interviews
Avoiding the need to read the advert in detail before each application

questions.hint: Prepared examples can be adapted.

questions.prompt: What do many successful candidates have in common?

options.text: They avoided applications with tests
They applied for only one advert and put all their effort into it
They never asked for feedback
They learned from earlier unsuccessful applications

questions.hint: Persistence and learning help.

items.title: L3: Pay, grades and what an advert tells you about the job
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; GOV.UK, Civil Service grades
items.body: The grade, salary and location in an advert tell you a lot about the job. The grade shows the level of responsibility. Entry-level roles are Administrative Assistant (AA) and Administrative Officer (AO). Executive Officer (EO) is the next level and often involves supervising a small area of work or handling more complex cases. Above that are Higher Executive Officer (HEO) and Senior Executive Officer (SEO). Salaries for the same grade can differ between departments, because each department sets its own pay within agreed limits. Pay in London is often higher than elsewhere, to reflect the higher cost of living, so the same grade may carry a different salary in London, Newcastle or Cardiff. The advert states the salary or the range, and often what the starting point is. It may also mention allowances, such as extra payments for some skills or locations. The advert says if the role is permanent or fixed term, and if it is full time, part time or flexible. It also says what the role involves day to day and what security checks apply. Use these details to judge whether the job suits you before applying. If you rely on a particular working pattern, for example school hours, check that the advert allows it. If it does not say, use the contact in the advert to ask.

options.text: Because London jobs require a degree

items.title: L3: Reserve lists, feedback and what happens after the interview
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: After the interviews, the panel scores each candidate against the criteria and the recruiting team compares the scores. The highest-scoring candidates who meet the standard are offered the available posts. If there are more successful candidates than vacancies, the department may place the others on a reserve list, sometimes called a merit list. If a similar job comes up within a set period, usually stated in the advert or the outcome email, the department can offer it to someone on the list without running a new competition. This saves time and money. Being on a reserve list does not guarantee an offer. It means you reached the standard but there was no post for you at that time. You may be told the outcome by email or phone. If you are unsuccessful, ask for feedback. It should tell you how you did against the criteria and where you could improve. Take notes and use them for the next application. If you are successful, you receive a conditional offer. The word conditional means it depends on the pre-employment checks. The email will say what to do next, such as providing identity documents and referee details by a stated date. Reply promptly and keep your phone and email checked. Do not tell your current employer until the offer is firm.

questions.prompt: What does the panel do after the interviews?

options.text: Starts the pre-employment checks for all applicants
Chooses candidates by drawing names
Sends all applicants a copy of the scores of others
Scores each candidate against the criteria

questions.hint: Scores are matched to the criteria.

questions.hint: It holds successful candidates for later vacancies.

items.title: L3: Pre-employment checks and why they take time
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Pre-employment checks protect the public, the department and the information it holds. They are run after a conditional offer, and they can take some weeks, so start gathering documents early. Identity is checked using original documents, such as a passport or a driving licence, plus proof of address such as a recent bank statement or utility bill. The right to work check confirms that you can legally work in the UK, and may involve an online share code if you have an immigration status. Employment history is checked for about the past three years, using referees such as employers, a university or a person who can confirm what you were doing. If you had time out, for example caring for a relative, you will be asked to explain it, and sometimes provide a person who can confirm it. Unspent criminal convictions are declared. Having a conviction does not always stop you being employed, but you must declare it honestly and the department will consider it. Some roles need more than the baseline: Counter Terrorist Check, Security Check or Developed Vetting. These involve extra questions and may take months. Delays often occur because referees are slow to reply or documents are missing. You can help by giving accurate contact details and answering requests quickly. Do not resign or make plans until you receive a confirmed start date.

items.title: L3: Security clearance and why jobs need it
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; National Security Vetting
items.body: Some Civil Service jobs involve access to sensitive information, secure places or national security work. For those, the department needs extra confidence about who is doing the job. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS, applies to everyone and confirms identity, right to work, employment history and unspent convictions. It is not a formal security clearance. National security vetting adds further levels. Counter Terrorist Check (CTC) is needed for some jobs which involve proximity to public figures or certain sites. Security Check (SC) is needed for jobs with longer-term or frequent access to secret assets. Developed Vetting (DV) is the most detailed, for roles with long-term, frequent and uncontrolled access to the most sensitive information. Each level involves more checks than the one below. The checks may include questions about finances, past addresses, family and associates, and an interview. A common requirement for SC and DV is a minimum period of residence in the UK, so a person who has recently arrived may not be eligible, however good their record. This is not a reflection on the person. The advert states the level, and vetting can take weeks or months, so the start date may be later than for roles that need only baseline checks. Be fully honest, because concealment is treated more seriously than the fact itself.

items.title: L3: Equality, discrimination and protected characteristics
items.source: Equality Act 2010, GOV.UK; Civil Service Commission
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination at work, including in recruitment. It lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Direct discrimination means treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic, for example refusing to interview a person because of their age. Indirect discrimination happens when a rule that applies to everyone puts people with a protected characteristic at a disadvantage and cannot be justified. For disabled people there is also a duty to make reasonable adjustments. Civil Service recruitment tries to prevent bias in several ways. Panels are trained and use scoring guides. Some departments use name-blind sifting, where the names of applicants are hidden from those who score the applications. Questions are the same for every candidate. Equal opportunities monitoring forms collect information such as gender, ethnicity and disability. These forms are usually separate from the scoring and are not seen by the people who sift or interview. Candidates can answer them or choose not to. The aim is to check, over many applications, whether certain groups are doing worse, so that unfair barriers can be found and removed. If you think you were treated unfairly, raise it with the department and, if needed, the Civil Service Commission.

options.text: Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic

questions.hint: It is less favourable treatment because of a characteristic.

items.title: L3: Honesty, the Civil Service Code and applications
items.source: Civil Service Code, GOV.UK; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out the standards expected of every civil servant. It has four core values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Integrity means putting the obligations of public service above your own interests. Honesty means being truthful and open. Objectivity means basing advice and decisions on rigorous analysis of the evidence. Impartiality means acting solely according to the merits of the case and serving equally well governments of different political persuasions. These values start to matter at the application stage. If you give false information, for example a qualification you do not hold, a job you did not do or a reason for a gap that is not true, you risk having the offer withdrawn. If a false statement is found after you start, it can lead to disciplinary action and dismissal. It is better to be honest, even about gaps or difficult circumstances. Departments are used to people with unusual careers, caring responsibilities, time out of work or a past that includes setbacks. Describe those facts plainly and focus on what you learned and can do now. In some cases, a deliberately false statement can also be treated as fraud, which is a criminal offence. When you complete forms, check every date and detail against your records. If you are unsure, say so or ask the contact in the advert.

items.title: L3: Flexible working, job share and caring responsibilities
items.source: GOV.UK, Flexible working; Civil Service Jobs adverts
items.body: Many Civil Service jobs can be done part time, as a job share or with flexible hours, though not all of them. Part time means working fewer hours than full time. In a job share two people share the duties of one full-time post, working different days or parts of the week, and handing over to each other. Flexible working may include flexible start and finish times, compressed hours (working the same hours over fewer days), or working from home for part of the week. Hybrid working means a mix of office and home. The advert says what is possible, and some roles state that applications for part-time or job-share working are welcome. Employees have a legal right to request flexible working, and the employer must consider the request reasonably. The employer can refuse for specific business reasons, but must treat the request seriously. People with caring responsibilities, such as for children or a relative with health needs, may find these options useful, but should check what the role requires. Some jobs, especially those that deal directly with the public, need set hours or someone present at set times. If you have set times you cannot work, raise it at the right moment, such as when you ask the contact named in the advert. Working patterns agreed at the start are normally written into your contract or offer.

items.title: L3: Staying safe from recruitment scams
items.source: Civil Service Jobs website; GOV.UK; Action Fraud guidance
items.body: Because Civil Service jobs are popular, scammers sometimes pretend to be recruiters. Knowing the signs helps you protect yourself. Real Civil Service recruitment never asks you to pay a fee to apply, be tested, or start work. Genuine adverts are on the Civil Service Jobs website, and official emails come from the departments and the website. Be suspicious of any message that offers a job without an application or interview, promises very high pay for little work, or comes from a free email address that does not look official. Scammers may also ask you to move the conversation to a messaging app, which is a warning sign. Never give out your bank details, your password or your national insurance number in response to an unexpected message. In a genuine process, identity documents are checked after a conditional offer and through the department's official channels, not by sending photographs to a stranger. If you receive a message you are unsure of, do not click links in it. Go to the Civil Service Jobs website directly and log in to check your account for messages. You can also contact the department using the contact in the advert. Report suspected fraud to Action Fraud. Tell the department as well, so it can warn other applicants. Do not feel embarrassed. Scammers are skilful and anyone can be caught out.

items.title: L3: Planning backwards from a closing date
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A closing date can feel far away on the day you find a vacancy, but good applications take time. A useful approach is to plan backwards. Start with the closing date and work back, deciding when each step should be done. For example, if an advert closes on a Friday evening, aim to submit by the Tuesday or Wednesday. That leaves a buffer for any problem with the website, your connection or your device. Before that, plan time to proof-read, ideally after a break so you read it freshly. Before that, set aside time to write the first draft. Before that, spend time reading the advert closely and listing the criteria or behaviours. Then choose which examples to use for each one. Write down more than you need and select the best. If a test follows the application, find out the date early and plan practice sessions. If the advert gives interview dates, check whether you will be available and arrange childcare or time off. Keep a list of all your applications with their closing dates. If two close in the same week, prioritise the one you most want and which fits your skills best. It is better to submit one strong application than three rushed ones. Last, give yourself a short reward for finishing. Small habits help you keep going.

items.title: L3: Contacting the department and asking questions
items.body: Every Civil Service advert gives a contact, often a named person or team with an email address, for questions about the job and for reasonable adjustments. Using the contact is normal, and it does not count against you. Good reasons to get in touch include checking whether a flexible working pattern is possible, asking about eligibility if you are unsure, asking for an accessible format, or checking a detail in the advert that is unclear. Questions about how the process works are fine too. Keep your message short and polite. State the job title and reference number, explain who you are and ask a clear question. For example: I am applying for the Administrative Officer role with reference number 12345. Could you tell me whether it can be done as a job share? Say thank you. Do not ask the contact to tell you how to answer a question on the form or to review your answers. They are not allowed to give an advantage to one candidate. Do not ask for the scoring guide or inside information about the panel. Keep a copy of the reply in case you need it later. If you do not get a reply in a few working days, and the closing date is near, send a short polite follow-up. If you have a disability, you can ask for a reasonable adjustment through the same contact and describe what would help.
